newsitem.title: GERMANY: Telekom must not be one-off event-bourse.
newsitem.headline: Telekom must not be one-off event-bourse.

text.p: The launch of shares in Deutsche Telekom AG has stimulated German investor interest in shares which must be cultivated and spread to other areas of the bourse, German bourse chief Werner Seifert said on Monday.
Seifert told a news conference: "This is a decisive contribution to strengthening the equity culture among private investors in Germany."
The five-times oversubscription of the shares stood in stark contrast to worries only a few months ago, that the market would be unable to absorb an issue of this size.
But he added that more must be done to keep the interest of traditionally cautious German investors alive.
"An equity culture does not come on its own, and cannot be created alone," he said, adding that the government, banks, and press had all played their part in making the Telekom issue a success.
Deutsche Boerse itself had responded by increasing capacities and opening hours, he added.
Further privatisations of this type were also needed to give the German share market increased depth and volume, he said, adding that it lagged far behind other world markets.

"As astounding as the dimensions of today's events appear, the Telekom privatisation must not remain a one-off event," adding that the German share market was still very small in comparison to other world markets.
The German share market's capitalisation totalled just 27.2 percent of gross domestic product compared with 78 percent in the United States and 124 percent in Britain, he added.
German investment funds have just 11 percent of their total capital invested in shares and ordinary citizens have put just 5.5 percent of their savings in stocks.

"There is considerable scope for improvement," said Seiffert, encouraging Germany's state governments to privatise where possible, adding that a well-functioning capital market was essential to give small, young companies access to funds.

Good investor relations, increased deregulation, investor-friendly tax conditions and an increasing emphasis on investment to finance retirement were all factors which could help the market grow further, he added.

Seiffert specially urged the government not to carry out plans to introduce a capital gains tax that would tax all appreciation of share prices. Until now share price gains were only taxed if the shares were sold within the first six months of ownership.
